widgets.title: Where the bell curve comes from
widgets.blurb: Each row of pegs nudges a ball one step left or right; where it lands is the sum of those nudges. Drop enough and you see how far many small random errors, added together, stray from zero.

widgets.title: Central Limit Theorem
widgets.blurb: Starts empty. Draw one sample at a time and watch its observations collapse to a mean that falls into the pile below — which goes normal whatever the population looks like, with spread σ/√n.

widgets.title: Uncertainty from one sample
widgets.blurb: You get one sample, never a population. Resample it with replacement — duplicates and all — and the spread of the resampled means stands in for a sampling distribution you could never observe. As well as your one sample represents the population, and no better.

widgets.title: Could chance alone have done this?
widgets.blurb: If the grouping meant nothing, any relabelling of the same numbers would be as likely. Pool the observations, deal them back, rebuild the difference — and p is simply how many of those shuffles reached what you actually saw, in red. Set the true effect to None and watch a false positive happen.
